newsitem.title: USA: Morris defends right to write White House memoir.
newsitem.headline: Morris defends right to write White House memoir.

text.p: President Clinton's former campaign chief strategist Dick Morris on Wednesday defended his decision to publish his memoirs without telling the White House, saying his lawyer advised him it was not necessary.

The Washington Post reported on Wednesday that Morris hid his plan to write the book by evading a White House request not to disclose what he learned as an insider. The Post added that a confidentiality agreement is part of the employment agreement staff members sign with the campaign.
It said Morris had signed one in 1995 but when that contract expired, he resisted signing a new agreement.

Morris, who resigned from the campaign after a sensationalist supermarket tabloid reported that he had an affair with a prostitute, said in a statement issued by his publisher that, "I consulted with an attorney last year who advised me that no disclosure of my plans to write a book was necessary.
"I would imagine that there will be dozens of books written by staffers, consultants and cabinet officials of their days in the Clinton administration."

He said that he spoke to the president last month about his plan to write "a public account of our experiences" and the president asked that he wait until after the elections to publish it and "that I treat the subject in a way that is 'right for you and right for me.' I agreed."
He added that he worked for the White House for 22 months, 18 of them without a contract and said he never was a public official and never took an oath of office.

"My book will be dignified, insightful, accurate, probing and I hope newsworthy. But it will not be inconsistent with my lifetime of loyality to William Jefferson Clinton who I believe to be one of our truly great presidents."
Random House has reportedly paid Morris $2.5 million for the book.
